title: Cell Theory and Cell Organelles
notes:
Cell Theory

The cell was discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665.

Statements of Cell Theory

  • All living organisms are composed of small living units called cells.
  • All cells are fundamentally similar in chemical composition and metabolic activities.
  • All cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula e cellula).
  • Cells are the structural and functional units of life.

Cellular Totipotency

The potentiality of vegetative plant cells to develop into a complete new individual organism.

The term was coined by Haberlandt (1902) and experimentally proved by F.C. Steward (1958). It forms the basis for plant tissue culture.

Types of Cells

Prokaryotic Cell

A cell lacking a nuclear membrane to enclose genetic material into an organized nucleus, and lacking membrane-bound organelles.

Characteristics:

  • Lack nuclear membrane.
  • Mitotic cell division is absent.
  • Plasma membrane forms inward folds called mesosomes.
  • Cytoplasmic streaming does not occur.
  • Respiration occurs through plasma membrane.

Eukaryotic Cell

A cell possessing a membrane-bound organized nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

Characteristics:

  • Mitotic apparatus present.
  • Cell division occurs via mitosis, meiosis, or amitosis.
  • Cytoplasmic streaming occurs.

Unicellular vs Multicellular Organisms

AspectUnicellularMulticellular
Body CompositionSingle cell carries out all life processes.Many cells; different cells carry out specialized functions.
Cell Size1 µm to 1 mm.5 µm to 100 µm.
Organelle AccommodationCell must be sufficiently large to accommodate all organelles.Cells are of various sizes tailored for specific functions.

Plant Cell vs Animal Cell

FeaturePlant CellAnimal Cell
Cell WallPresent (cellulosic outer wall).Absent (enclosed only by plasma membrane).
PlastidsPresent.Absent.
VacuolesLarge central vacuole present in mature cells.Small or absent altogether.
CentrioleAbsent.Present.
CrystalsMay be present.Usually absent.

Cell Components and Organelles

Cell organelles: Living sub-cellular structures in cytoplasm with definite form and function (protoplasmic bodies).

Cell inclusions: Non-living ergastic/deutoplasmic substances formed as metabolic products in cytoplasm.

Cell Wall

Outermost rigid, protective layer in plants, bacteria, fungi, cyanobacteria, and protists.

Layers:

  • Middle lamella
  • Primary cell wall
  • Secondary cell wall
  • Associated structure
    • Plasmodesmata — channels connecting adjacent plant cells.

Functions:

  • Provides mechanical strength
  • Maintains cell shape
  • Prevents undue expansion
  • Enzymatic activities

Cell Coat

Layer outside the plasma membrane consisting of glycoproteins and carbohydrates (glycocalyx); in some cells (e.g. diatoms) strengthened by silica/calcium salts.

Functions:

  • Protects plasma membrane
  • Gives shape
  • Helps in cell recognition and immunity

Protoplasm

Living substance of cell; divided into nucleoplasm (in nucleus) and cytoplasm (extra-nuclear).

Composition:

ConstituentPercentage
Water75–90%
Proteins7–20%
Carbohydrates1–2%
Lipids2–3%
Inorganic materials1%
RNA0.7%
DNA0.4%

Plasma Membrane

Thin, elastic, semi-permeable membrane surrounding cytoplasm.

Structural models:

  • Sandwich model: Trilaminar structure of phospholipid bilayer sandwiched between two monolayer protein coats.
  • Fluid mosaic model: Phospholipids are fluid-like; proteins are embedded (intrinsic) or superficial (extrinsic).

Functions:

  • Provides shape to animal cells.
  • Protects cell contents.
  • Endocytosis, exocytosis, pinocytosis (cell drinking), phagocytosis (cell eating).
  • Locomotion (e.g., pseudopodia in Amoeba).

Mitochondria

Discovered by Kolliker (1857). Double-membrane-bound organelle; inner membrane folds into cristae; space between is perimitochondrial space.

Functions:

  • Site of aerobic respiration — the powerhouse of the cell.
  • Self-replicating organelle due to its own DNA, RNA, and ribosomes.
  • Regulates calcium ion concentration.
  • Site of thermogenesis and yolk formation in ova.

Plastids

Largest plant cell organelles; absent in animals, fungi, and prokaryotes.

  • Chloroplast: Green plastid; double-membrane bound with fluid stroma inside. Functions: site of photosynthesis ('Kitchen of the cell'), maintains O2 and CO2 balance, reduces global warming.
  • Chromoplast: Coloured plastids containing carotenoid pigments (carotenes, xanthophylls) in vesicles; gives colour to flowers and fruits.
  • Leucoplast: Colourless plastids in underground parts; store reserve food (starch, oils, proteins).

Endoplasmic Reticulum

Network of interconnected cisternae, tubules, and vesicles in cytoplasm.

FeatureRough ER (RER)Smooth ER (SER)
RibosomesCovered with ribosomes.Not covered with ribosomes.
FunctionActive in protein synthesis.Active in lipid/steroid synthesis.
StabilityMore stable.Less stable.

Golgi Complex

Discovered by Camillo Golgi. Consists of cisternae, vesicles, tubules, and golgian vacuoles. Called dictyosomes in plant cells.

Functions:

  • Forms primary lysosomes
  • Secretes hormones
  • Biosynthesis of glycoproteins

Ribosomes

Non-membrane-bound nucleoprotein granules consisting of RNA and protein. Occur as 70S (30S + 50S) in prokaryotes and 80S (40S + 60S) in eukaryotes.

Functions:

  • Protein factories of the cell
  • Site for protein synthesis

Lysosomes

Single-membrane bound vesicles containing ~40 hydrolytic enzymes. Known for polymorphism.

Forms: Primary lysosomes, secondary lysosomes, residual bodies, autophagosomes.

Functions:

  • Intra and extracellular digestion
  • Destroys pathogens
  • Acts as 'Suicidal bags' of cell via autolysis during starvation

Cilia and Flagella

Hair-like motile structures originating from basal bodies with a 9+2 tubulin microtubule arrangement (axoneme).

FeatureCiliaFlagella
SizeShort (5–10 µm)Long (up to 150 µm)
NumberNumerous, cover whole bodyFewer, usually at anterior end
MotionSweeping/rowing motionUndulatory motion

Vacuoles

Non-cytoplasmic fluid-filled spaces enclosed by tonoplast. Larger and fewer in plant cells.

Types: Food vacuoles, gas vacuoles, contractile vacuoles, sap vacuoles.

Functions:

  • Store water, minerals, food, and waste
  • Gas vacuoles provide buoyancy

Nucleus

Brain of the cell containing genetic material. Absent in mammalian mature RBCs and sieve tube cells.

Components:

  • Nuclear membrane (Karyotheca)
  • Nucleoplasm (Nuclear sap)
  • Chromatin fibers
  • Nucleolus

Chromatin types:

  • Heterochromatin: Darkly stained, tightly coiled, genetically inert.
  • Euchromatin: Lightly stained, loosely coiled, genetically active.

Chromosomes

Condensed chromatin fibers formed during cell division consisting of DNA and proteins.

Types by centromere position: Metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric.
examples:
**Q1: Cell Theory**

Who discovered the cell, and who coined the term cellular totipotency?

**Solution:** The cell was discovered by Robert Hooke (1665). Cellular totipotency was coined by Haberlandt (1902) and experimentally proved by F.C. Steward (1958).

**Q2: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic**

What is the fundamental difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?

**Solution:** Prokaryotic cells lack a nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles (division by constriction, mesosomes present), whereas eukaryotic cells possess a membrane-bound organized nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

**Q3: Powerhouse of the Cell**

Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell, who discovered it, and why is it self-replicating?

**Solution:** Mitochondria (Kolliker, 1857). It is the site of aerobic respiration, so it is called the powerhouse; it is self-replicating because it has its own DNA, RNA, and ribosomes.

**Q4: Lysosomes**

Why are lysosomes called the 'suicidal bags' of the cell?

**Solution:** During starvation or injury, lysosomes burst and release their ~40 hydrolytic enzymes to digest the cell's own contents — autolysis — hence the name.

**Q5: Chromatin Types**

Distinguish between heterochromatin and euchromatin.

**Solution:** Heterochromatin is darkly stained, tightly coiled, and genetically inert; euchromatin is lightly stained, loosely coiled, and genetically active.

keyPoints: Mitochondria (Kolliker, 1857) = 'powerhouse of the cell'; self-replicating with own DNA, RNA and ribosomes; regulates calcium ion concentration.
Chloroplast = 'kitchen of the cell' — site of photosynthesis; maintains O2/CO2 balance.
Ribosomes: 70S (30S + 50S) in prokaryotes, 80S (40S + 60S) in eukaryotes — the protein factories.
Lysosomes = 'suicidal bags' (autolysis during starvation) with ~40 hydrolytic enzymes.
Cilia and flagella: 9+2 tubulin arrangement (axoneme); cilia short (5–10 µm), flagella long (up to 150 µm).
Heterochromatin: darkly stained, tightly coiled, genetically inert. Euchromatin: lightly stained, loosely coiled, genetically active.
Prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles; mesosomes are inward folds of the plasma membrane.
Golgi complex = dictyosomes in plant cells; forms primary lysosomes and glycoproteins.
summary: Cells are the structural and functional units of life (Robert Hooke, 1665). Prokaryotic cells lack a nuclear membrane and organelles; eukaryotic cells have both. Key organelles include the plasma membrane (fluid mosaic model), mitochondria (powerhouse, Kolliker 1857), plastids (chloroplast, chromoplast, leucoplast), ER (RER protein / SER lipid synthesis), Golgi complex (dictyosomes), ribosomes (70S/80S), lysosomes (suicidal bags), cilia/flagella (9+2), vacuoles (tonoplast) and the nucleus (hetero/euchromatin). Cellular totipotency (Haberlandt 1902, Steward 1958) is the basis of plant tissue culture.
